title: Git, Collaboration & Craft
description: Git workflows and branching, code review etiquette, technical debt and refactoring cadence, and documentation as a first-class artifact.

lessons.title: Git Workflows and Branching
lessons.description: Why teams branch, what trunk-based development means, and why frequent small merges ease conflicts.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why teams branch, what trunk-based development means, and why frequent small merges ease conflict resolution.

sections.title: 🌿 Why branch at all
sections.content: A **branch** is an independent line of development. Without branching, everyone would edit the same shared history directly, so an unfinished feature or an experiment that doesn't pan out would sit mixed in with everything else. Branching lets work happen in isolation — a feature branch, a bugfix branch, an experiment — without disturbing the main line of history until that work is ready to join it.

sections.title: 🔀 A common workflow
sections.content:
**Feature branches**: each unit of work (a feature, a fix) gets its own branch, created off the main line, developed and reviewed there, then merged back in once it's ready.

**Trunk-based development** takes this further: branches are short-lived (often merged within a day or two), and everyone merges frequently into a single shared "trunk" (often called `main`). The core idea is that the longer a branch lives without merging, the further it drifts from what everyone else is doing, and the more painful the eventual merge becomes — so trunk-based teams deliberately keep that drift small by merging often.

sections.title: 💥 Merge conflicts are information, not failure
sections.content: A **merge conflict** happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file in incompatible ways, and Git can't automatically decide which version to keep. This isn't a sign something went wrong — it's Git correctly noticing that two people's intentions overlap and asking a human to reconcile them. Frequent small merges make conflicts easier to resolve for a simple reason: a conflict between two changes made an hour apart is small and easy to reason about, while a conflict between two branches that diverged three weeks ago can span dozens of interacting changes.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Git conflict markers can look intimidating the first time you see them, so here's what they actually represent and how to read them.

```python
# A conflict is Git showing you both versions of the same lines, side by side.
# This is what a conflicted file looks like after a failed automatic merge:

conflicted_file = '''\
def get_discount(user):
<<<<<<< HEAD (your current branch)
    if user.is_premium:
        return 0.20
=======
    if user.years_active >= 2:
        return 0.15
>>>>>>> feature/loyalty-discount (the branch being merged in)
    return 0.0
'''

def parse_conflict_sections(text):
    """Splits a conflicted block into 'ours' and 'theirs' for inspection."""
    ours, theirs = [], []
    section = None
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("<<<<<<<"):
            section = "ours"
            continue
        if line.startswith("======="):
            section = "theirs"
            continue
        if line.startswith(">>>>>>>"):
            section = None
            continue
        if section == "ours":
            ours.append(line)
        elif section == "theirs":
            theirs.append(line)
    return ours, theirs

ours, theirs = parse_conflict_sections(conflicted_file)
print("our version:", [l.strip() for l in ours])
print("their version:", [l.strip() for l in theirs])
# A real resolution here is neither -- it's deciding the actual intended logic,
# e.g. applying whichever discount is larger, or keeping both as separate tiers.
```

The `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers aren't an error — they're Git literally showing you both sides of the disagreement so a human can decide the real intent. `parse_conflict_sections` just mechanically separates "ours" from "theirs"; the actual resolution (which discount rule should win, or whether both should apply) is a judgment call no tool can make for you.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Letting a branch live for weeks without merging.** The longer a branch diverges from the trunk, the larger and harder-to-reason-about the eventual conflict becomes — small, frequent merges keep conflicts small too.

**Resolving a conflict by blindly picking one side.** A conflict means two changes overlap; mechanically keeping "ours" or "theirs" without understanding both intents can silently discard a real fix or feature.

**Treating a conflict as a sign something is broken.** A conflict is Git doing its job — flagging genuine overlap for a human to resolve, not evidence of a mistake.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of branching in Git?
options: To permanently delete old code
To let work happen in isolation without disturbing the main line of history until it's ready
To automatically merge conflicting changes
To speed up the compiler
questions.explanation: Branching creates an independent line of development, so unfinished features or experiments can develop in isolation without affecting the shared main history until they're ready to merge in.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind trunk-based development?
options: Branches should never be created
Branches should be short-lived and merged frequently into a single shared trunk to minimize drift
Only one developer should ever commit to the trunk
Trunk-based development eliminates the need for code review
questions.explanation: Trunk-based development keeps branches short-lived and merges them frequently, based on the idea that the longer a branch lives without merging, the further it drifts and the more painful the eventual merge becomes.

questions.question: Why do frequent small merges make conflict resolution easier?
options: Because Git resolves small conflicts automatically
Because a conflict between changes made close together in time is smaller and easier to reason about than one between branches that diverged for weeks
Because small merges never produce conflicts
Because frequent merges disable conflict detection
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a conflict between two changes made an hour apart is small and simple, while a conflict between branches that diverged three weeks ago can span dozens of interacting changes.

questions.question: In the code example, what do the `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` markers represent?
options: Syntax errors in the code
The boundaries of the two conflicting versions of the same lines, from each branch
Comments left by a code reviewer
Deleted lines that Git is warning about
questions.explanation: The markers delimit the conflicting block: `<<<<<<<` through `=======` is the current branch's version ("ours"), and `=======` through `>>>>>>>` is the incoming branch's version ("theirs").

questions.question: What does `parse_conflict_sections` return for the example `conflicted_file`?
options: Two identical lists
The 'ours' list containing the is_premium check, and the 'theirs' list containing the years_active check
An empty list for both
A single merged list combining both conditions
questions.explanation: Based on the conflict markers, the HEAD ("ours") section contains the `if user.is_premium` line, and the incoming branch ("theirs") section contains the `if user.years_active >= 2` line.

questions.question: According to the code example's closing comment, what does a real resolution to this conflict require?
options: Automatically picking Git's default suggestion
A human judgment call about the actual intended logic, such as applying whichever discount is larger or keeping both as separate tiers
Deleting both versions and starting over
Reverting to the last commit before the conflict
questions.explanation: The comment explicitly states the real resolution is neither side alone — it's a judgment call about the actual intended business logic, which no tool can make automatically.

questions.question: Why is letting a branch live for weeks without merging flagged as a common mistake?
options: Because Git deletes branches automatically after a week
Because the longer a branch diverges from the trunk, the larger and harder the eventual conflict becomes
Because long-lived branches use more disk space
Because it violates Git's built-in size limits
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that divergence compounds over time, so a branch left unmerged for weeks accumulates a much larger, harder-to-reason-about conflict than frequent small merges would produce.

questions.question: Why is blindly picking one side ("ours" or "theirs") to resolve a conflict considered a mistake?
options: Because Git doesn't allow choosing a side
Because it can silently discard a real fix or feature from the side that wasn't kept, without reconciling both intents
Because it always causes a syntax error
Because it deletes the entire file
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that mechanically keeping one side without understanding both changes' intent risks silently losing a genuine fix or feature that was in the discarded side.

lessons.title: Code Review Etiquette
lessons.description: Why small, well-described pull requests get better review, and why reviewing too slowly is also a problem.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why small, well-described pull requests get better review, and why reviewing too slowly is also a problem.

sections.title: 📏 Keep changes small and focused
sections.content: A pull request that changes 30 lines across one clear concern gets read carefully. A pull request that changes 2,000 lines across five unrelated concerns gets skimmed, rubber-stamped, or avoided entirely — there's simply too much for a reviewer to hold in their head at once, so the quality of review drops as the size grows. Splitting a large change into a sequence of small, focused PRs — even if they land in the same day — almost always produces better review than one giant PR.

sections.title: 📝 Write a clear description, not just a diff
sections.content: The diff shows *what* changed. A good PR description explains *why*: what problem this solves, what approach was chosen and why (especially if an alternative was considered and rejected), and anything a reviewer should pay special attention to. A reviewer who understands the reasoning behind a change can evaluate whether it's the right change — a reviewer who only sees the diff can only check whether the code looks locally correct.

sections.title: ⏱️ Review promptly, but don't rush
sections.content: A pull request sitting unreviewed for days blocks the author, encourages context-switching costs (the author has moved on to something else by the time feedback arrives), and, ironically, tends to produce worse reviews — by the time someone finally looks, there's schedule pressure to just approve it. The fix isn't to review instantly and carelessly, either; it's to build review into the normal cadence of the day, so PRs get a real look within hours, not days.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a small, illustrative model of the size/quality relationship the lesson describes — not a claim about exact numbers, but a way to make the shape of the trade-off concrete.

```python
def estimate_review_thoroughness(lines_changed, unrelated_concerns):
    """
    A toy model: thoroughness starts at 100 and drops as a PR grows in size
    and mixes more unrelated concerns. Purely illustrative, not a real metric.
    """
    size_penalty = min(lines_changed // 50, 70)       # caps out, but still hurts a lot
    concern_penalty = unrelated_concerns * 10
    return max(100 - size_penalty - concern_penalty, 5)

prs = [
    ("small, focused PR", 30, 0),
    ("medium PR, one concern", 300, 0),
    ("large PR, multiple concerns", 2000, 4),
]

for name, lines, concerns in prs:
    score = estimate_review_thoroughness(lines, concerns)
    print(f"{name}: estimated thoroughness = {score}")
# small, focused PR: 100
# medium PR, one concern: 94
# large PR, multiple concerns: 20
```

The exact numbers aren't the point — `estimate_review_thoroughness` is a toy, not a real metric — but the shape is: the small, focused PR keeps its full score, the medium single-concern PR drops only slightly even at 300 lines, and the large PR mixing four unrelated concerns collapses to 20, illustrating why size *and* mixed concerns compound against review quality rather than just adding up linearly.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Bundling unrelated changes into one PR.** A refactor mixed in with a bug fix mixed in with a new feature forces the reviewer to evaluate three different things at once, and makes it hard to revert just one of them later if needed.

**Writing a description that just restates the diff.** "Updated the file" or "fixed the bug" gives a reviewer no more information than the diff already shows — the description's job is to add the *why*.

**Letting PRs sit unreviewed for days, then rushing through them.** Both extremes — never reviewing and reviewing too fast under pressure — produce worse outcomes than a steady, prompt cadence.

questions.question: Why do small, focused pull requests tend to get reviewed more carefully than large ones?
options: Because small PRs are always bug-free
Because a reviewer can hold a small, focused change in their head, while a large PR with many concerns is too much to review carefully
Because Git only allows small PRs to be merged
Because large PRs are automatically rejected by CI
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a small PR covering one clear concern gets read carefully, while a very large PR with unrelated concerns tends to get skimmed or rubber-stamped because there's too much for a reviewer to hold in mind at once.

questions.question: What should a good PR description explain that the diff alone does not?
options: The exact line count changed
Why the change was made and what alternatives were considered
The reviewer's name
The programming language used
questions.explanation: The lesson states the diff shows what changed, but a good description explains the why — the problem being solved, the approach chosen, and what a reviewer should pay attention to.

questions.question: Why is reviewing too slowly identified as a problem, according to the lesson?
options: Because slow reviews are technically impossible
Because it blocks the author, creates context-switching costs, and tends to produce rushed, lower-quality reviews under later schedule pressure
Because Git automatically closes old pull requests
Because slow reviews always introduce security bugs
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a PR sitting unreviewed for days blocks the author and creates costs, and ironically tends to produce worse reviews once someone finally looks, due to schedule pressure to just approve it.

questions.question: In the code example, what estimated thoroughness score does the "medium PR, one concern" (300 lines, 0 unrelated concerns) receive?
questions.explanation: With 300 lines, `size_penalty = min(300 // 50, 70) = 6`, and `concern_penalty = 0 * 10 = 0`, so the score is `100 - 6 - 0 = 94`.

questions.question: Why does the "large PR, multiple concerns" example score much lower (20) than the medium PR (94), even though its line count is less than 7x larger?
options: Because the function has a bug
Because both the size penalty and the concern penalty apply and compound together, not just the larger line count alone
Because large PRs are scored randomly
Because 2000 lines exceeds a hard limit that always returns 20
questions.explanation: The large PR combines a size penalty (`min(2000 // 50, 70) = 40`) with a concern penalty (`4 * 10 = 40`), totaling `100 - 40 - 40 = 20` — the combination of both penalties, not line count alone, is what drives the score down sharply.

questions.question: Why is bundling a refactor, a bug fix, and a new feature into one PR called a mistake?
options: Because Git cannot technically process more than one type of change per PR
Because it forces the reviewer to evaluate three different things at once and makes it harder to revert just one of them later
Because refactors are never allowed in pull requests
Because bug fixes must always be their own repository
questions.explanation: The lesson explains bundling unrelated changes forces a reviewer to evaluate multiple different things simultaneously and complicates reverting just one of them if something goes wrong later.

questions.question: Why does a PR description that just restates the diff (like "fixed the bug") fail to do its job?
options: Because it's too short to compile
Because it gives the reviewer no more information than the diff already shows, missing the why behind the change
Because it violates a strict character limit
Because reviewers cannot read diffs
questions.explanation: The lesson states the description's job is to add the why — the reasoning and context — so a description that only restates what the diff already shows provides no additional value to the reviewer.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say the fix for slow reviews isn't to review instantly and carelessly instead?
options: Because instant reviews are technically impossible
Because both extremes — never reviewing and rushing through review under pressure — produce worse outcomes than building review into a steady, prompt cadence
Because careless reviews are actually more thorough
Because reviewers should only review once a week regardless of speed
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes explicitly frame this as two failure modes on the same spectrum: letting PRs sit unreviewed for days and then rushing through them are both worse than a steady cadence that gives PRs a real look within hours.

lessons.title: Technical Debt and Refactoring Cadence
lessons.description: Deliberate vs. accidental technical debt, and why a regular repayment cadence beats occasional cleanup sprints.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Distinguish deliberate from accidental technical debt, and explain why a regular repayment cadence beats occasional cleanup sprints.

sections.title: 💳 The financial metaphor, taken seriously
sections.content: **Technical debt** is a deliberate or accidental shortcut in code that makes the immediate work faster, at the cost of making future work slower — exactly like financial debt lets you have something now in exchange for paying more later. And like financial debt, it accrues **interest**: the longer a shortcut stays in place, the more code gets built on top of it, and the more expensive it becomes to fix later, because now the fix has to account for everything built on top.

sections.title: 🎯 Deliberate debt vs. accidental debt
sections.content:
**Deliberate debt** is a conscious trade-off: "we're hardcoding this configuration to ship by Friday, and we know we'll need to generalize it later." This is a legitimate engineering decision when it's made consciously and, ideally, tracked somewhere so it doesn't get forgotten.

**Accidental debt** accumulates without anyone deciding it should: copy-pasted code that was never refactored into a shared function, a workaround for a bug that was never revisited after the bug was fixed elsewhere, an architecture that made sense for the original scope but never got updated as requirements grew. Accidental debt is more dangerous precisely because no one chose it — it just happens if nobody watches for it.

sections.title: 📅 Why a repayment cadence matters
sections.content: Treating debt repayment as an occasional "cleanup sprint" tends to fail in practice: cleanup work competes with feature work for priority, and feature work almost always wins in the short term, so the cleanup sprint keeps getting postponed while debt keeps accruing interest. A **regular cadence** — a fixed percentage of every sprint, or a standing weekly slot — treats debt repayment as a normal, ongoing cost of doing business rather than a special event that has to win a priority fight against every new feature request.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a small simulation contrasting the "occasional cleanup sprint" approach against a "steady cadence" approach, tracking accumulated debt over the same 12 sprints.

```python
def simulate_debt(sprints, new_debt_per_sprint, cleanup_schedule):
    """
    cleanup_schedule: a function(sprint_number) -> amount of debt paid down that sprint.
    Returns the debt level at the end of each sprint.
    """
    debt = 0
    history = []
    for sprint in range(1, sprints + 1):
        debt += new_debt_per_sprint
        debt -= cleanup_schedule(sprint)
        debt = max(debt, 0)
        history.append(debt)
    return history

def occasional_cleanup(sprint):
    # A big cleanup sprint only every 4 sprints -- and it keeps slipping in practice,
    # represented here by sprint 8's cleanup being skipped under feature pressure.
    if sprint == 4:
        return 15
    if sprint == 12:
        return 15
    return 0

def steady_cadence(sprint):
    return 4  # a fixed amount paid down every single sprint

occasional = simulate_debt(12, 5, occasional_cleanup)
steady = simulate_debt(12, 5, steady_cadence)

print("occasional cleanup, debt over time:", occasional)
print("steady cadence, debt over time:      ", steady)
print("peak debt -- occasional:", max(occasional), " steady:", max(steady))
```

Both scenarios accrue the same 5 units of new debt every sprint, but they pay it down very differently: `occasional_cleanup` only pays anything on sprints 4 and 12 (mirroring a cleanup sprint that keeps slipping), so debt climbs unchecked for long stretches in between; `steady_cadence` pays down 4 units every single sprint, keeping debt low and roughly flat. Printing `max(...)` for each makes the peak-debt gap concrete — the occasional approach lets debt climb far higher before it's ever addressed.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Taking on debt without tracking it anywhere.** A shortcut that only lives in one person's memory gets forgotten the moment that person moves to another project — write it down.

**Treating all debt repayment as a special "cleanup sprint" event.** This keeps losing the priority fight against new feature work, which is exactly why debt tends to grow unchecked under this model.

**Confusing "deliberate" with "consequence-free."** Choosing to take on debt consciously is still taking on debt — it still accrues interest and still needs a plan to pay it down, just on a schedule the team chose rather than one forced on them later.

questions.question: What does technical debt trade in the short term for a cost later, according to the financial metaphor?
options: Faster immediate work for slower future work
Better code quality for worse performance
More tests for fewer features
Lower cost for higher security risk
questions.explanation: The lesson describes technical debt as a shortcut that makes immediate work faster at the cost of making future work slower, directly mirroring how financial debt trades present benefit for future cost.

questions.question: What is the key difference between deliberate and accidental technical debt?
options: Deliberate debt is always worse than accidental debt
Deliberate debt is a conscious, ideally tracked trade-off, while accidental debt accumulates without anyone deciding it should
Accidental debt doesn't accrue interest
Deliberate debt cannot be paid down later
questions.explanation: The lesson defines deliberate debt as a conscious engineering decision, ideally tracked, whereas accidental debt accumulates unnoticed — like copy-pasted code or an outdated architecture — which is why it's described as more dangerous.

questions.question: Why does treating debt repayment as an occasional "cleanup sprint" tend to fail in practice?
options: Because cleanup sprints are technically impossible to schedule
Because cleanup work competes with feature work for priority, and feature work almost always wins in the short term, so cleanup keeps getting postponed
Because debt cannot be measured
Because cleanup sprints always introduce new bugs
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that occasional cleanup sprints have to win a priority fight against feature work each time, and feature work tends to win in the short term, so the cleanup keeps slipping while debt keeps accruing interest.

questions.question: In the code example, on which sprints does `occasional_cleanup` pay down any debt?
options: Every sprint
Only sprints 4 and 12
Only sprint 1
Never
questions.explanation: `occasional_cleanup` returns 15 only when `sprint == 4` or `sprint == 12`, and 0 on every other sprint — modeling a cleanup effort that happens rarely and keeps slipping in between.

questions.question: How much debt does `steady_cadence` pay down on each individual sprint?
questions.explanation: `steady_cadence` always returns 4, regardless of the sprint number, representing a fixed amount paid down consistently every sprint.

questions.question: Why does the code example print `max(occasional)` and `max(steady)` specifically?
options: To find which sprint has the most new debt added
To compare the peak debt level each approach reaches, showing the occasional approach lets debt climb much higher before being addressed
To count the total number of sprints
To verify the simulation has no bugs
questions.explanation: The lesson's explanation notes this makes the "peak-debt gap" concrete — since occasional_cleanup lets debt climb unchecked for long stretches between sprints 4 and 12, its peak debt is expected to be substantially higher than steady_cadence's.

questions.question: Why is taking on debt without tracking it anywhere flagged as a common mistake?
options: Because untracked debt automatically doubles in size
Because a shortcut that only lives in one person's memory gets forgotten once that person moves to another project
Because Git requires all debt to be documented
Because untracked debt is illegal under most engineering standards
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that debt tracked only in someone's memory disappears from the team's awareness the moment that person is no longer around to remember it, making it effectively invisible.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against confusing "deliberate" debt with "consequence-free" debt?
options: Because deliberate debt is actually accidental debt in disguise
Because choosing to take on debt consciously doesn't exempt it from accruing interest or needing a repayment plan
Because deliberate debt cannot be tracked
Because only accidental debt needs to be repaid
questions.explanation: The lesson clarifies that even consciously chosen debt still accrues interest and still needs a plan to pay it down — being deliberate about taking it on doesn't make it free, just chosen on the team's own schedule.

lessons.title: Documentation as a First-Class Artifact
lessons.description: Why different documentation serves different readers, why it rots, and how this closes the course's arc.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why different kinds of documentation serve different readers, why documentation rots, and how this lesson closes the course's arc.

sections.title: 📚 Different documentation serves different readers
sections.content:
Documentation isn't one thing — different kinds serve different readers at different moments:

- A **README** orients a newcomer: what this project is, how to get it running, where to look next.
- **Inline comments** explain *why* a specific piece of code does something non-obvious, for the next person (often you, in six months) reading that exact line.
- **Architecture docs** explain how the pieces fit together at a higher level than any single file shows, for someone trying to understand the system's shape before diving into any one part of it.
- **API docs** tell an external consumer exactly what a given endpoint or function expects and returns, without requiring them to read the implementation at all.

Writing documentation without asking "who is this for, and what do they need at this moment" tends to produce writing that satisfies no one particularly well.

sections.title: 🕰️ Documentation rots if it's not maintained like code
sections.content: Documentation that describes behavior which has since changed is often worse than no documentation at all — a reader who trusts it gets actively misled, whereas a reader who finds nothing at least knows to go check the code directly. Documentation stays trustworthy only when updating it is treated as part of the change that makes it stale — bundled into the same pull request that changes the behavior, not deferred to "we'll update the docs later," which in practice often means never.

sections.title: 🎓 Closing this course's arc
sections.content: This course started with clean code and naming — the smallest unit of clarity, a single well-named function. It moved through data structures and algorithms — the tools for solving problems efficiently. It moved through system design — how those tools compose into whole systems. It moved through testing — how you know those systems actually work. And it ends here, with documentation and collaboration — because none of the technical skill in the earlier lessons matters much if it can't be understood, maintained, and built on by the people working alongside you, including your future self. Good software engineering was never just about writing code that works once — it's about writing code, and the material around it, that keeps working as other people (and time) act on it.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a small, concrete illustration of documentation rot — and the one habit that prevents it.

```python
# --- The function, and its docstring, at time of writing ---

def get_active_users(users, days=30):
    """Return users active in the last 30 days."""
    return [u for u in users if u["days_since_active"] <= days]

users = [
    {"name": "Alice", "days_since_active": 5},
    {"name": "Bob", "days_since_active": 45},
    {"name": "Carol", "days_since_active": 60},
]

print("with default window:", [u["name"] for u in get_active_users(users)])
# ['Alice'] -- matches the docstring's '30 days' claim

# --- Six months later, someone changes the default without updating the docstring ---

def get_active_users_v2(users, days=90):
    """Return users active in the last 30 days."""  # <- now WRONG, still says 30
    return [u for u in users if u["days_since_active"] <= days]

print("with changed default:", [u["name"] for u in get_active_users_v2(users)])
# ['Alice', 'Bob'] -- the docstring says 30 days, but the real window is now 90
print("docstring still claims:", get_active_users_v2.__doc__)
```

`get_active_users` and its docstring agree at first: the default window is 30 days, and the printed result matches. `get_active_users_v2` is exactly the documentation-rot scenario — the default changed to 90, but the docstring was never touched, so it now actively misleads anyone who trusts it: Bob shows up as "active" under the new 90-day window while the docs still promise a 30-day one. The fix is process, not tooling — the docstring update belongs in the very same change that adjusted `days`.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Writing one kind of documentation for every audience.** A README written like an architecture doc overwhelms a newcomer trying to get the project running; an architecture doc written like a README leaves an experienced engineer without the detail they need.

**Deferring doc updates to "later."** In practice, "we'll update the docs later" very often means never — the only reliable way to keep documentation accurate is bundling its update into the same change that made it stale.

**Trusting documentation more than the code when the two disagree.** If a docstring and the actual implementation contradict each other, the code is what actually runs — treat the mismatch as a bug in the documentation to fix, not evidence to act on as-is.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what does a README primarily do?
options: Explain why a specific line of code exists
Orient a newcomer to what the project is, how to run it, and where to look next
Define an external API's exact request and response shape
Describe the system's architecture in full technical depth
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the README as serving a newcomer specifically: orienting them to what the project is, how to get it running, and where to go next.

questions.question: Why can outdated documentation be worse than no documentation at all?
options: Because outdated documentation takes up disk space
Because a reader who trusts outdated docs gets actively misled, whereas a reader who finds nothing knows to check the code directly
Because documentation always slows down the build process
Because outdated docs are illegal under most licenses
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that trusting stale documentation actively misleads a reader, while the absence of documentation at least signals that the code itself needs to be checked directly.

questions.question: How does this lesson frame its place in the arc of the whole Software Engineering course?
options: As an unrelated bonus topic tacked onto the end
As the closing lesson, arguing that none of the earlier technical skills matter much if the resulting work can't be understood and maintained by others
As a replacement for the testing module
As a prerequisite that should have come first
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly walks back through clean code, data structures/algorithms, system design, and testing, framing documentation and collaboration as the closing piece that makes all of that earlier work maintainable by others.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `get_active_users(users)` return with its default arguments, and why?
options: An empty list, because no users are active
['Alice'], because only Alice has days_since_active <= 30
['Alice', 'Bob'], because the window is actually 90 days
All three users, because the docstring is inaccurate
questions.explanation: With the default `days=30`, only Alice (`days_since_active: 5`) falls within the window; Bob (45) and Carol (60) do not, so the result is `['Alice']`, matching what the docstring claims.

questions.question: What specifically makes `get_active_users_v2` an example of documentation rot?
options: It has a syntax error
Its default changed from 30 to 90 days, but its docstring still says '30 days', so the docs no longer match the actual behavior
It removed the docstring entirely
It returns a different data type than the original function
questions.explanation: The function's `days` default was changed to 90, but the docstring was left saying "last 30 days" — the documentation and the actual behavior have diverged, which is precisely what documentation rot means.

questions.question: According to the code example's closing explanation, what is the actual fix for documentation rot?
options: A better documentation generation tool
Bundling the docstring update into the very same change that adjusted the behavior it describes
Removing all docstrings to avoid the risk
Running the code more often
questions.explanation: The lesson states explicitly that the fix is process, not tooling — updating the docstring should happen in the same pull request that changes the behavior, rather than being deferred.

questions.question: Why is writing one kind of documentation for every audience called a mistake?
options: Because only one kind of documentation is allowed per project
Because each kind of documentation serves a different reader's needs, so a mismatch (like a README written as an architecture doc) fails to serve anyone well
Because it takes too long to write multiple documents
Because documentation tools only support one format
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes point out that a README written like an architecture doc overwhelms a newcomer, while an architecture doc written like a README lacks the detail an experienced engineer needs — each audience needs its own appropriate form.

questions.question: If a docstring and the actual code implementation disagree, what does the lesson say you should trust?
options: The docstring, since it represents the intended design
The code, since that's what actually runs — treat the mismatch as a bug in the documentation
Neither — the function should be deleted
Whichever was written more recently, regardless of which is code
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes explicitly state that when a docstring and the implementation contradict each other, the code is what actually runs, so the mismatch should be treated as a documentation bug to fix, not something to act on as-is.
